pathetic.drift: Once meant moving or touching; now usually weak and contemptible.

inadvertent.literal: not turning your mind to it

specious.drift: Once meant handsome; now means looking right but being wrong.

pragmatic.literal: relating to affairs or things done

gregarious.literal: full of flocks, tending to gather in groups

mortality.literal: the state or condition of being subject to death

palliate.drift: Once meant to cloak or conceal; now means to ease suffering or soften the severity of a problem.

abortive.literal: causing an attempt to miscarry or fail
abortive.drift: Once meant causing stillbirth or miscarriage; now means ending without success or completion.

decade.literal: a set or period of ten

culminate.literal: to cause to reach the highest point

gradual.literal: characterized by steps, proceeding by degrees

obsolescence.literal: process of falling out of use

modify.literal: make or form according to a measure

originate.literal: to give rise to; to begin

charisma.drift: Once referred to a divinely bestowed gift; now usually means personal charm or magnetism.

dilettante.literal: one who takes pleasure in an activity

humility.literal: the state of being humble or lowly

phlegmatic.literal: characterized by phlegm, the humor associated with coldness and sluggishness

urbane.literal: of or pertaining to the city; refined in city manners

contrite.drift: Once meant physically crushed; now means deeply sorry and accepting responsibility.

cynical.drift: Originally referred to dog-like behavior; now means distrustful of people’s motives.

forlorn.drift: Once meant lost; now means feeling sadly abandoned or alone.

indignant.literal: not worthy; being angry at what is unworthy

repress.drift: Originally meant to suppress or force down; now commonly means to keep feelings or memories from being openly expressed or consciously acknowledged.

sensitive.literal: having the quality of feeling or perceiving

serenity.literal: state of being calm and peaceful

revere.drift: Once conveyed reverence; now means to regard with deep respect and admiration.

umbrage.drift: Originally meant “shade” or “shadow”; now means a feeling of offence or resentment.

conflagration.literal: a burning together or widespread burning

confront.literal: face together, bring face to face

duress.literal: hardship or a state of compulsion

impede.literal: to shackle the feet, hinder progress

ingratiate.literal: to move or act for favor

subjugate.literal: bring under the yoke; make subject

awesome.drift: Once meant inspiring awe; now commonly means excellent or impressive.

deprecate.drift: Originally meant to pray against an impending evil; now means to condemn strongly.

egregious.drift: Originally meant distinguished or eminent; now means extremely bad and shocking.

excoriate.literal: take the skin off; criticize harshly

florid.drift: Once meant flowering or flowery; now often means excessively ornate or decorative.

gratuitous.drift: Once meant freely given; now means given without sufficient reason or justification.

impeccable.literal: not able to err or sin

ethics.literal: the study of character or moral nature

milieu.drift: Originally meant the middle place or central position; now refers to a surrounding social, cultural, or professional environment.

propinquity.literal: nearness or the state of being nearby

technology.drift: Originally meant the systematic treatment of grammar; now means the practical application of scientific knowledge and methods.

venerate.literal: to worship or hold in reverence

aphoristic.literal: characterized by a statement or saying

disseminate.literal: to scatter seed in all directions

euphemism.literal: a word or expression of good omen, avoiding harsh speech

polemic.drift: Originally concerned with warfare or disputes; now chiefly means forceful argumentative criticism.

rhetoric.literal: of or relating to a speaker

scurrilous.drift: Once described buffoon-like or jocular behavior; now means vulgar and maliciously insulting.

analogous.literal: having a corresponding proportion or likeness

antithesis.drift: Originally referred to the arrangement of opposing words in rhetoric; now means an idea or approach that directly opposes another.

arbitrary.literal: depending on a judge or personal decision
arbitrary.drift: Once meaning determined by a judge; now often means based on whim, chance, or an unexplained rule.

complex.drift: Once meant woven or intertwined; now commonly means intricate or difficult.

evaluate.literal: bring out the strength or worth of

facile.literal: able to be done or made

indiscriminate.drift: Once meant not divided or separated; now means lacking careful distinctions.

ingenious.literal: full of productive or natural capacity

obviate.literal: meet in the way, so head off

rudimentary.literal: relating to a beginning or first attempt

ruminate.literal: turning over repeatedly in the mind

volition.literal: willing; the act of wishing or intending

delude.literal: mock or deceive by playing someone false

duplicity.literal: the state or condition of being double or twofold

insidious.literal: sitting in wait, artful or deceitful
insidious.drift: Originally meant cunning or deceitful; now emphasizes harm that develops gradually and remains hidden.

plausible.literal: able to be applauded or accepted

prevaricate.literal: to walk crookedly or play a false part

sophistry.literal: the craft of a clever talker

liquidation.literal: making liquid; the process of turning into a liquid

stipulate.literal: to state as a required condition or formal promise
